characterList.description: A white woman, wearing glasses and a grey cardigan. She is running for the Court of Common Pleas.
characterList.name: Jennifer Schultz

characterList.description: A young African American girl wearing a school uniform.
characterList.name: Jade Lindow

content_metadata.description: A video presenting Jennifer Schultz's campaign for the Court of Common Pleas, focusing on her advocacy for justice, youth empowerment, and restorative justice.

qAndA.question: What is the color of Jennifer Schultz’s campaign flyer?

qAndA.answer: Grumblethorpe, a historic house in Germantown.
qAndA.question: What is the name of the organization Jennifer volunteers at?
According to Jennifer, what percentage of people without a lawyer are evicted?

qAndA.answer: Ensuring access to justice for everyone, regardless of their background or financial situation.

activities.description: Jade Lindow introduces herself and the 'Close the Creek' event
Jennifer Schultz introduces herself and her campaign
Jade asks Jennifer who she is
Jennifer describes her work as an attorney at Community Legal Services
Jennifer explains her work helping people with foreclosure, taxes, and debt
Jade asks why Jennifer wants to be a judge

characterInteraction.description: Jade Lindow is interviewing Jennifer Schultz about her campaign and experience.

mood.description: Neutral - Curious, Content. The setting is simple and neutral. There's a sense of curiosity as Jade Lindow interviews Jennifer Schultz. Jennifer's tone is professional and informative, contributing to a content mood.

narrativeProgression.description: Jennifer Schultz introduces herself and her campaign for judge.
Jennifer describes her work as an attorney and her passion for helping people in need of legal representation.

activities.description: Jennifer explains why access to justice is crucial for a fair system
Jennifer shares statistics about evictions with and without lawyers
Jennifer emphasizes the need for judges to bridge the gap in legal representation
Jade asks about Jennifer's values regarding youth and children
Jennifer discusses her volunteer work with youth and women

characterInteraction.description: The interview continues, with Jade Lindow asking about Jennifer's personal values.

mood.description: Neutral - Pensive, Content. The discussion about access to justice introduces a slightly more serious and pensive tone. Jennifer's passion for helping youth and women contributes to a more content mood towards the end of the scene.

narrativeProgression.description: Jennifer highlights the importance of a fair justice system with equal representation for all, regardless of income.
Jennifer talks about her commitment to youth, evidenced by her volunteer activities.

scenes.thematicElements: Access to Justice: The scene emphasizes the importance of legal representation for a fair justice system and the need to address the disparity between those who can afford lawyers and those who cannot. Youth Empowerment: Jennifer's volunteer work highlights the importance of investing in and supporting youth to ensure their success and future opportunities.
scenes.title: Access to Justice & Youth

activities.description: Jade asks Jennifer about restorative justice
Jennifer explains the concept of restorative justice and its increasing importance
Jennifer discusses the shift from punishment-focused to community-focused justice
Jennifer explains how restorative justice aims to help both victims and those convicted of crimes to move forward

characterInteraction.description: Jade Lindow continues to ask thought-provoking questions to Jennifer Schultz.

mood.description: Neutral - Pensive. The discussion of restorative justice introduces a contemplative and reflective tone.

narrativeProgression.description: Jennifer elaborates on the importance of restorative justice, contrasting it with the traditional punishment-centered approach.
Jennifer explains the goals of restorative justice, emphasizing its focus on healing and moving forward for all involved.

scenes.thematicElements: Restorative Justice: This scene focuses on a shift in the criminal justice system towards restorative justice, which emphasizes repairing harm and rebuilding communities instead of solely focusing on punishment.
scenes.title: Restorative Justice

activities.description: Jade asks Jennifer for final thoughts
Jennifer reminds viewers of her name, campaign, and button number

characterInteraction.description: The interview ends with polite and friendly closing remarks.

mood.description: Positive - Grateful, Happy. The scene concludes with a friendly and positive tone, expressing gratitude for the interview.

narrativeProgression.description: Jennifer Schultz reiterates her campaign message and encourages viewers to vote for her.

climax.description: Jennifer Schultz's closing remarks reiterating her campaign message and asking for votes.

storylines.description: The video presents a narrative story showcasing Jennifer Schultz as a candidate for judge.

content_metadata.title: Jennifer Schultz's Campaign for Judge

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, my name is Jaila and I'm when you are.
Hi, I'm Jennifer Schultz.
I'm running for Court of Common, please.
And welcome to Close the Creek.
Thank you, it's great to be here tonight.
Who are you?
So I'm an attorney.
I work at community legal services.
And actually, just right down the street on the same block, it brought in Yuri.
And I've been there for over a decade, so that's more than 10 years.
I'm in something called the Home Ownership and Consumer Rights Unit.
Now that means I help people save their homes when they're having problems with foreclosures
and property taxes.
I also help people who are having problems with student loans and other kinds of debt.
Why do you want to be a judge?
My whole career has been about helping people who cannot afford an attorney, making sure
that they get adequate representation so that our system can work fairly because our justice
system works in the idea that you have two sides called an adversary system, and that
allows them to find the truth.
And if you don't have those two sides evenly matched, it doesn't work as well.
And we know that we did a recent study in our landlord tenant courts, and we know that
if you have a lawyer, you only get evicted about 5% of the time.
But when you don't have a lawyer, it's more than 70% of the time.
And that means our justice system isn't working the way that it should.
Even though myself and my colleagues work really hard and do a great job for our clients,
we're not able to help every person.
There are too many people who need help.
And judges really need to help close that gap and make sure that the system works for
everybody.
So I want to make sure that everybody is able to get access to justice in our country.
What are your vials on youth and children?
My values?
Yes.
So actually, I really care a lot about youth, and a lot of my volunteer activities have been
really focused on that.
I volunteer at a local historic house called Grumblethorpe in Germantown.
And the reason that I got so involved there is they have a youth program for middle school
and high schoolers.
And it's a place where they can learn about history and also learn skills that they can
take with them in their life.
And I'm a huge believer that knowledge is power.
So over the years, I volunteered for school career days and school mentorship programs.
I also participate in a women's group called American Association of University Women.
And in that program, I've done a lot of work around ways that we can help make sure that
girls and young women are able to excel and have the same opportunities as everyone
else in our society.
So that's something that I care a lot about.
And I know that we have to always work.
It takes a village and we're all part of making sure that youth are able to be fully participatory
in our society.
Here are restorative justice to you.
So the idea of restorative justice is really something that's being talked about more
and more.
And I think that's a good thing.
I think that in our ideas that sometimes we shift too far in one direction.
We talk about that as a pendulum.
And eventually we realize maybe we went too far and we need to go back the other way.
And for a long time in our country, we've been focused on punishment and tough on crime.
And what we're realizing is that harms communities.
It doesn't help victims.
It doesn't help people who've done things that are wrong.
And it doesn't help those families and the other people who rely upon people who have
been convicted of crimes.
Understanding that the people who are in a situation are going to be ongoing members of
our community and finding ways that we can help all of those people move forward after
a crime has been committed is really the goal of restorative justice.
Last thoughts?
Sure.
I just want everyone to remember I'm Jennifer Schultz.
Jennifer Judge.
I'm button number four.
And I hope you remember me on May 21.
Thank you so much.
It was great talking with you tonight.
Nice to meet you.
Thank you.
